clue.text: Just a quarter of this state would be fine (8)

definitions.text: Just a quarter of this state would be fine

blocks.clueFragment: Just a quarter of this state
blocks.note: reads as a slice of territory, but it is the first quarter of the state's name, two letters of eight
those two letters spell a short word meaning fine, all right

annotation.surface: A wry remark that you would settle for only a small slice of some American state.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a comment about territory, but the quarter is of the word: OK is two letters out of eight.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by wordplay on the name itself: the state is the answer, and its first two letters are the 'fine' the clue promises.

clue.text: Note is circulated at the workplace (2-4)

indicators.note: passed around, so the letters move about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

annotation.surface: An office memo being passed round the staff.
annotation.walkthrough: A memo that is circulated at work is exactly the office picture, so the anagram hides in plain sight.
annotation.definitionFit: On-site work is done at the workplace itself.

clue.text: One high-flying fashionable poet (6)

blocks.note: the skylark sings as it climbs high
in = fashionable

annotation.surface: A trendy poet enjoying high-flying success.
annotation.walkthrough: 'High-flying' sounds like career success; here it is a bird.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Philip Larkin, author of The Whitsun Weddings, is one English poet among many.

clue.text: Family should hope to move without pressure (9)

indicators.note: the letters are set moving into a new order
leave out the letter that follows

blocks.note: the raw letters
P = pressure, removed

annotation.surface: A family hoping to move house without the stress.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about house-hunting, which even plants HOUSE in the answer; pressure is the P taken out before rearranging.
annotation.definitionFit: A household is the family living together under one roof.

clue.text: Party game for conservatoire professors? (7,6)

blocks.note: the game where players grab a seat when the music stops
a professor holds a chair, and at a music college those chairs are musical

annotation.surface: Suggesting a party game for the staff of a music college.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: a chair is a professorship, so professors of music hold musical chairs.
annotation.definitionFit: Musical chairs is the children's party game of scrambling for seats.

clue.text: Ranges of jewellery items (6)

blocks.note: ranges as in lines of mountains, not a shop's product lines
linked metal necklaces or bracelets

annotation.surface: A jeweller's product lines.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ranges of jewellery' reads as a shop's stock; split it into mountain ranges and jewellery items.
annotation.definitionFit: Chains are ranges of mountains and also linked necklaces.

clue.text: Japanese work hard, assiduous in keeping up with the leaders (5)

indicators.note: leaders are the front letters of the words

blocks.note: first letters of Hard Assiduous In Keeping Up

annotation.surface: Japanese workers toiling hard to keep pace with the market leaders.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Japanese work hard' reads as a sentence about workers; 'work' belongs with 'Japanese' as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A haiku is a short Japanese poem, a literary work.

clue.text: Lock away troublemaker, absolutely not set up (8)

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: an imp is a little mischief-maker
no sir! = absolutely not

annotation.surface: Someone saying a troublemaker should be locked away, and it's certainly not a stitch-up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Set up' suggests being framed; in a down answer it means turn the letters upward.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: putting someone in prison is locking them away.

clue.text: Fast mover, first in shop to collect computer equipment (8)

indicators.note: take the opening letter of the next word

blocks.note: first letter of shop
a printer is computer equipment

annotation.surface: A speedy customer, first into the shop to pick up some computer kit.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a shopper racing in; the fast mover is the answer itself.
annotation.definitionFit: A sprinter is a runner built for speed.

clue.text: He provided waltzes as Truss danced (7)

indicators.note: the letters move to new places, as dancers do

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: A composer supplying the waltz music while Liz Truss took to the floor.
annotation.walkthrough: Liz Truss is a former British prime minister; her name here is just letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Johann Strauss II is the composer famed for Viennese waltzes such as The Blue Danube.

clue.text: Briskly cheerful person preparing potatoes? (7)

blocks.note: lively and cheery in manner
someone who cuts potatoes into chips

annotation.surface: A bright, bustling cook peeling spuds in the kitchen.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the invented sense: one who chips potatoes. Chips here are British chips, thick fries.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain, slightly informal synonym for lively good cheer, paired with an invented sense: one who chips potatoes.

clue.text: Soon abort scan, having broken instrument (13)

indicators.note: the letters are broken up and reassembled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: A technician about to stop a scan because the machine is faulty.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a medical or technical scan gone wrong; 'instrument' looks like a scanning device but is musical.
annotation.definitionFit: The contrabassoon is the deepest woodwind instrument of the orchestra.

clue.text: So shy after being bitten? (5)

blocks.note: reads as 'very shy'; 'so' actually stands in for a word of degree from a proverb
points to the proverb about being bitten once and then being wary

annotation.surface: Wondering whether someone is timid because they got bitten.
annotation.walkthrough: The proverb 'once bitten, twice shy' supplies the answer: after being bitten you are twice shy, so 'so' stands for TWICE.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: in 'once bitten, twice shy' the word paired with shy after the bite is the answer, so it replaces 'so'.

clue.text: Roman soldier expecting congratulatory telegram? (9)

blocks.note: an officer commanding a hundred men
someone reaching a hundred, who in Britain gets a message from the monarch

annotation.surface: A Roman legionary oddly waiting for a message of congratulations.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain, people turning 100 traditionally receive a congratulatory telegram (now a card) from the monarch; the question mark admits the playful sense of centurion as a centenarian.
annotation.definitionFit: A centurion commanded a century of Roman soldiers.

clue.text: Arrested advocate for peace getting the bird (8,4)

blocks.note: collared = arrested, in police slang
a dove argues for peace, the opposite of a hawk

annotation.surface: A peace activist being arrested and then given the bird by the crowd.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Getting the bird' sounds like being jeered; here the bird is the definition itself.
annotation.definitionFit: The collared dove is a common grey-brown dove with a black neck ring.

clue.text: Not scared to relocate here? (9)

indicators.note: the letters move to new positions

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: Someone bold enough to move house to a particular town.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is just 'here', a place, which the question mark admits is loose. Doncaster is a town in South Yorkshire, England.
annotation.definitionFit: Doncaster is a place someone might move to, and the clue points at it as 'here'.

clue.text: One dies in court, making a point (4,4)

definitions.text: One dies in court, making a point

blocks.note: sounds like a death in a law court; in sport, a ball 'dies' when it loses its bounce on the court
sounds like winning an argument; in tennis or squash it is winning a rally

annotation.surface: A death in a courtroom that somehow proves someone's argument.
annotation.walkthrough: The court is a tennis or squash court, not a law court, and 'dies' is the ball losing all pace.
annotation.definitionFit: A sporting term: a softly played shot that barely clears the net and dies in the opponent's court, often winning the rally outright.

clue.text: Hearing test (8)

blocks.note: the faculty or sense of hearing, a formal word
a trial performance

annotation.walkthrough: 'Hearing test' looks like one medical phrase; split it into two meanings of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Audition means both the faculty of hearing and a performer's tryout.

clue.text: What you don’t see when driving is crazy (5,3,4)

definitions.text: What you don’t see when driving

blocks.clueFragment: What you don’t see when driving
blocks.note: the road beyond a curve is hidden
a British idiom for mad

annotation.surface: A driver's complaint that it's mad what you can't see from the road.
annotation.walkthrough: Round the bend is British slang for mad; the first half is literal, what lies beyond a curve in the road.
annotation.definitionFit: Round the bend means both out of sight past a curve and crazy.

clue.text: Band, note, played at funfair (6)

definitions.note: the definition describes the answer, a game played at funfairs, rather than naming it

blocks.note: a hoop is a band, as on a barrel
la, the sixth note of the sol-fa scale

annotation.surface: A band playing a note at the funfair.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Band' and 'played' suggest musicians; the band is a ring. Hoopla is the fairground game of throwing rings over prizes.
annotation.definitionFit: Hoopla is a game played at fairs, tossing hoops over prizes.

clue.text: Scots girl has energy after cold drink (6)

indicators.note: the energy letter comes after the drink

blocks.note: lassi is a chilled yoghurt drink from South Asia
E = energy, as in physics

annotation.surface: A Scottish girl getting a boost after a cold drink.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'drink' is not a Scotch; it is lassi, the Indian yoghurt drink.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: the Scots diminutive of lass, a girl.

clue.text: Prudish stars get together for elections (9)

blocks.note: prim = prudish
Aries, the Ram, a constellation and star sign

annotation.surface: Straitlaced celebrities joining forces for an election campaign.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stars' reads as celebrities; it is the constellation Aries.
annotation.definitionFit: Primaries are elections to choose a party's candidates.

clue.text: A mortgage said to be unique (5)

indicators.note: spoken, so go by sound, not spelling

blocks.note: a mortgage is a loan

annotation.surface: A claim that a certain mortgage deal is one of a kind.
annotation.walkthrough: Alone in the sense 'unmatched', as in standing alone.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of standing by oneself, without equal.

clue.text: A traveller’s distinctive fragrance (5)

blocks.note: used as is
the Roma are a traditionally travelling people; the 's is traveller is

annotation.surface: The characteristic scent of a traveller.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe s reads as possession but stands for 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An aroma is a distinctive, usually pleasant, smell.

clue.text: Outrageously wicked criminal in house (7)

indicators.note: the letters are treated criminally, out of order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: An appallingly wicked burglar inside a home.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like a noun for the villain; it is the adjective telling you to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Heinous means shockingly evil.

clue.text: After a few weeks, work for an army type? (7)

indicators.note: the work comes after the month

blocks.note: a month is a few weeks; OCT is the calendar abbreviation for October
opus = a work

annotation.surface: Taking up military service after a few weeks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Army type' suggests a soldier; read it as arm-y, having many arms, and the octopus has eight.
annotation.definitionFit: An octopus, with eight arms, is jokingly an army creature.

clue.text: Youthful follower of steam engines (6)

blocks.note: young, as of someone with few years behind them
the wagon behind a locomotive carrying coal and water

annotation.surface: A young railway enthusiast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Follower' suggests a trainspotter; it is the car that literally follows the engine.
annotation.definitionFit: Tender means young, as in 'at a tender age'.

clue.text: In credit, comfort is to grow (8)

blocks.note: used as is
CR = credit, as on a bank statement
ease = comfort

annotation.surface: Financial advice that being in the black lets your comfort grow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In credit' reads as one banking phrase but supplies two pieces, IN and the abbreviation CR.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to become larger or more numerous.
